findings.title: Unauthenticated log injection through the password-reset user field
findings.evidence: id = request.form.get(u'user') on line 610, then on line 616 log.info(u'Password reset requested for user "{}"'.format(id)) with no neutralisation between the two. The same value reaches line 650, log.info(u'User requested reset link for unknown user: {}'.format(id)). Nothing on the path strips or escapes control characters: request.form values are decoded form data and may contain CR and LF. The logger is CKAN's default line-oriented logging (logging.getLogger(__name__), formatters configured in ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl), so one newline in the value produces a second record. The route is reachable with no credential: RequestResetView is exempted from the login gate at ckan/views/user.py:80-85, where before_request allows action in ('login','request_reset','perform_reset') to proceed after a NotAuthorized site_read. The legacy Pylons twin carries the same defect at ckan/controllers/user.py:482 and 486. The pack's log_escaper.py flags all four lines as UNCLEARED.
findings.impact: An anonymous caller who can POST to /user/reset writes arbitrary forged lines into the application log. That corrupts the audit trail for exactly the flow an incident responder reads first (account recovery), lets an attacker manufacture plausible 'Emailing reset link to user: admin' records to misdirect an investigation, and can defeat or trigger prefix-matching alert rules. Where the log is rendered by a viewer that does not escape, or parsed by an aggregator that splits on newlines, this reaches further: injected markup or fabricated structured fields land in another product's trust boundary.
findings.recommendation: Neutralise before the sink rather than at it. Replace the .format() interpolation with a value that cannot carry control characters - e.g. log a repr, or run the value through a strict [A-Za-z0-9@._-]{0,255} filter before logging, or emit one JSON object per event with a formatter that escapes control characters and confirm the consumer parses that format. Applying the fix at 616 alone is not enough: 650, 654 and the Pylons twin at ckan/controllers/user.py:482/486 carry the same defect and the same value.
findings.verification: Local and inert: POST user=bob%0A2026-08-24 INFO Emailing reset link to user: admin to /user/reset against a local instance, then count the lines the logger produced. One input, two records, is the finding. Repeat with <b> if any viewer renders the log.

triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the value is request.form.get('user') at ckan/views/user.py:610, unauthenticated and unconstrained
triage.FP-03: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the sink is a line-oriented text logger, not a structured one; no formatter in ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl escapes control characters
triage.FP-09: DOES_NOT_HOLD - .format() into a logging message is exactly what it looks like
triage.FP-10: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the accountability loss is the impact, and it is not merely informational because the surrounding lines are the recovery-flow audit trail

findings.open_questions: Whether any deployment renders these logs in an HTML viewer would raise this to stored XSS; that is outside this tree.

findings.title: Log injection through the raw request path, on every request
findings.evidence: Line 425 reads url = request.environ['PATH_INFO'] and line 426 does log.info(' %s %s render time %.3f seconds' % (status_code, url, r_time)). PATH_INFO is the percent-decoded path under PEP 3333, so GET /%0d%0aFORGED arrives at this line already containing CR LF. The after-request hook runs for every Flask request (registered at ckan/config/middleware/flask_app.py, app.after_request), so the sink is unauthenticated and unconditional. The contrast inside this same tree is what makes it decidable: the Pylons twin at ckan/lib/base.py:313 logs request.environ['CKAN_CURRENT_URL'], and CKAN_CURRENT_URL is built at ckan/views/__init__.py:319-321 as '/'.join(quote(pce, '') for pce in path_info.split('/')) - percent-quoted per segment, so a newline there becomes %0A. One of the two paths neutralises, the other does not. A second site, ckan/config/middleware/__init__.py:116, logs environ.get('PATH_INFO') raw at debug level. log_escaper.py flags line 426 as UNCLEARED.
findings.impact: Any anonymous HTTP request forges arbitrary access-log records. This is the highest-volume injection point in the tree - one crafted URL per record, no authentication, no state - and access logs are the record most likely to be shipped to a shared aggregator or a SIEM, so the forged lines cross into another system's trust boundary. It also permits log flooding and the poisoning of any prefix- or regex-based detection built on this format.
findings.recommendation: Log the quoted form the Pylons branch already computes - reuse request.environ['CKAN_CURRENT_URL'], or apply the same six.moves.urllib.parse.quote per segment before the sink. Do the same at ckan/config/middleware/__init__.py:116 and 152. Do not fix this by switching from % to a deferred %s: the interpolation style is not what makes it safe.
findings.verification: Local: curl --path-as-is 'http://localhost:5000/%0d%0a2026-08-24 INFO forged' and count the records the logger emitted for that one request.

triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - PATH_INFO is caller-chosen and decoded by the WSGI layer
triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the quoting control exists in this codebase (ckan/views/__init__.py:319) but is not on this path

findings.open_questions: Some WSGI servers reject %0A in the request line before the application sees it; the fix should not depend on which server is deployed.

findings.title: API key and Authorization header written to the log in cleartext
findings.evidence: log.debug(u'Received API Key: %s' % apikey) on line 277, executed on every request that carries a credential. The value logged is whatever lines 261-275 collected: the X-CKAN-API-Key header, or the raw HTTP_AUTHORIZATION environ value. The spaces filter on line 273-275 is applied only to the non-prefixed 'Authorization' environ key, not to HTTP_AUTHORIZATION on line 270, so a full 'Bearer <jwt>' or 'Basic <base64(user:pass)>' header is logged verbatim. The value is a live credential: line 280 looks it up as model.User.apikey and line 283 falls through to api_token.get_user_from_token(apikey), i.e. the JWT API token. Note that the pack's own log_escaper.py marks this line CLEARED - it credits the six.ensure_text() call on line 276 as a neutraliser. That credit is wrong for this class, which is why the pack tells you not to read a cleared line as a clearance; I am reporting it on the reading, not on the tool.
findings.impact: Anyone who can read the application log - an operator, a log-shipping agent, a backup, a shared aggregator, a support bundle - obtains working API tokens and can act as the token's owner, including a sysadmin. This is privilege escalation through a channel that is normally treated as lower-sensitivity than the database, and it is silent: the token owner has no way to notice. Basic credentials arriving via HTTP_AUTHORIZATION are logged in the same line.
findings.recommendation: Remove the value from the message. If a diagnostic is needed, log a stable non-reversible handle (first 4 characters plus a truncated HMAC, or the resolved user id after lookup) and never the token itself. Apply the spaces filter to HTTP_AUTHORIZATION as well, so Basic credentials cannot reach this code path at all.
findings.verification: Local: issue a request carrying X-CKAN-API-Key with a synthetic token at log level DEBUG and grep the log for the token. Then add a regression test asserting the token does not appear.

triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the value is a live credential from the request headers
triage.FP-04: DOES_NOT_HOLD - this is not debug-gated code; it is a debug-*level* log statement in the shipped request path, and CKAN deployments commonly run DEBUG logging (ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl ships a [loggers] section operators routinely set to DEBUG)
triage.FP-07: DOES_NOT_HOLD - an API token is the definition of security-valuable data
triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no redaction filter exists anywhere in ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl

findings.open_questions: None. Severity would drop to medium in a deployment that pins the logger to INFO and can show that, but the default logging config ships no redaction filter either way.

findings.title: Whole API request body logged at debug and echoed back in error responses, including passwords
findings.evidence: log.debug(u'Request data extracted: %r', request_data) on line 220, reached by every /api/action/<fn> call. request_data is the full decoded body, so a POST to /api/action/user_create or /api/action/user_update logs the plaintext 'password' field, and a POST to /api/action/api_token_create logs the token request. The same dict is then returned to the caller inside error bodies: ckan/views/api.py:286 puts 'data': request_data into the DataError response and line 305 logs it again on ValidationError. The legacy twin is ckan/controllers/api.py:373-375, 406 and 430. No redaction filter exists: grep for filter_parameters / redact / sanitiz across ckan/config returns nothing.
findings.impact: Plaintext user passwords and token-creation payloads land in the application log, and are additionally reflected to the caller in error bodies. Log readers obtain credentials directly; the reflection also widens what an attacker learns from a malformed request. Password reuse makes the log copy usable beyond this system.
findings.recommendation: Redact before logging: log the key names and the body size, not the values, or run request_data through an allowlist-aware filter that masks password, password1, password2, apikey, token and Authorization. Stop putting request_data into the DataError response body; return the validation errors only.
findings.verification: Local: POST a synthetic user_create at DEBUG log level and grep the log for the password value; assert absence in a regression test.

triage.FP-07: DOES_NOT_HOLD - passwords are security-valuable by definition
triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no redaction processor is configured anywhere in this tree
triage.FP-04: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the statement ships in the request path

findings.open_questions: None.

findings.title: Stored XSS: resource metadata JSON injected verbatim into a script element
findings.impact: Any account that can create or edit a resource stores script that executes for every visitor who opens that resource's view page, on the CKAN origin. Because the auth cookie is HttpOnly by default the payload cannot read it directly, but it runs with the victim's session and can drive the API as the victim - so a sysadmin viewing a submitted dataset is a full site takeover (create a sysadmin, mint an API token via /api/action/api_token_create). On sites where anonymous or self-service dataset creation is enabled, the precondition is 'anyone'.
findings.recommendation: Do not emit JSON into an HTML script element with a raw serializer. Either escape the three characters that matter before marking the value safe - replace '<' with '\u003c', '>' with '\u003e' and '&' with '\u0026' (and U+2028/U+2029) inside the JSON string - or, better, move the payload out of the markup: emit <script type="application/json" id="preload-resource">, which is still not safe against </script>, or set the value from a data-* attribute where Jinja's normal attribute escaping applies and read it with JSON.parse in the module. Fix ckan/templates/dataviewer/base.html:8 and ckanext/textview/theme/templates/text_view.html:16-18 together; they are the same construct.
findings.verification: Local: set a resource description to , open the text_view page, and check window.__xss in the console. Inert marker only, no exfiltration.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no CSP is emitted anywhere in this tree (see F16), so nothing constrains inline execution
triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - resource fields are user-supplied and validated only for unicode-safety
triage.FP-10: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the impact reaches the viewing user

findings.open_questions: ckanext/textview is not enabled by default; ckan/templates/dataviewer/base.html is core and is the base of every dataviewer template, so the class does not depend on that plugin.

findings.title: Uploaded resource served with an attacker-chosen Content-Type, giving stored XSS on the CKAN origin
findings.evidence: download() serves an uploaded file with flask.send_file(filepath) on line 177 and then, on lines 178-179, overrides the type: if rsc.get(u'mimetype'): resp.headers[u'Content-Type'] = rsc[u'mimetype']. 'mimetype' is a plain user-writable resource field - ckan/logic/schema.py:48 declares 'mimetype': [ignore_missing, unicode_safe], with no allowlist and no pattern. The file body is equally unconstrained: ResourceUpload (ckan/lib/uploader.py:225-300) performs no content or extension check at all. Note the asymmetry inside the same file: the sibling Upload class does have Upload.verify_type() at ckan/lib/uploader.py:196-224, which reads the magic bytes and enforces ckan.upload.<type>.mimetypes (default image/png,image/gif,image/jpeg) - so the group/user image path is gated and the resource path is not. No X-Content-Type-Options and no Content-Disposition is set anywhere in the tree (grep for nosniff returns nothing).
findings.impact: A user who can add a resource uploads an HTML file, sets mimetype to text/html, and /dataset/<id>/resource/<rid>/download renders it as a page on the CKAN origin, in the victim's session. Same consequence as F5 - session-riding API calls as the victim, sysadmin takeover if a sysadmin opens it - but with a fully attacker-controlled document rather than an injected fragment, so it is not constrained by any surrounding markup. It also makes the CKAN domain a host for arbitrary phishing content.
findings.recommendation: Two independent fixes, both worth having. (1) Do not trust the stored mimetype for the response: map it through an allowlist of inert types and fall back to application/octet-stream, and add X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff plus Content-Disposition: attachment on this route. (2) Give ResourceUpload the content check that Upload already has - call the same magic-based verify_type() with a configurable allowlist. Serving uploads from a separate origin would remove the class entirely.
findings.verification: Local: upload a file whose body is <script>window.__xss=1</script>, set mimetype=text/html via /api/action/resource_update, fetch the download URL and observe the response Content-Type and whether the marker executes.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no nosniff, no CSP, no Content-Disposition on this route
triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - mimetype is [ignore_missing, unicode_safe] at ckan/logic/schema.py:48
triage.FP-05: DOES_NOT_HOLD - serving uploads is intended, serving them as text/html on the session origin is not; and there is no separate storage origin in this configuration

findings.open_questions: None.

findings.title: SSRF: the resource proxy fetches any user-supplied URL with no scheme or host restriction
findings.evidence: url = resource[u'url'] on line 39 is the resource's URL field, writable by any user who can create a resource (ckan/logic/schema.py:38, 'url': [ignore_missing, unicode_safe, remove_whitespace]). The only validation is lines 41-43: parts = urlsplit(url); if not parts.scheme or not parts.netloc: abort(409). That requires a scheme and a host and constrains neither. The server then issues requests.head(url) on line 49 and requests.get(url, stream=True) on lines 55 and 69, from its own network position. requests follows redirects by default and no allow_redirects=False appears on any of the three calls, so even a host filter added at the entry point would be defeated by a 302. There is no allowlist, no private-range check, and no egress policy anywhere in this tree. The route is ckanext/resourceproxy/blueprint.py:110, /dataset/<id>/resource/<resource_id>/proxy, and proxy_view passes c.user as the context - the resource_show authorization is against the resource, not against the URL.
findings.impact: The CKAN server is turned into a request forwarder inside its own trust zone: the cloud metadata service at 169.254.169.254 (instance credentials), Redis and Solr and Postgres admin interfaces on the internal network, and anything bound to 127.0.0.1. The response body is streamed back to the caller (lines 74-76), so this is a fully readable SSRF, not blind. On a cloud deployment with an instance role this is a path to the deployment's cloud credentials.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the host before connecting and refuse loopback, link-local, private and unique-local ranges (both A and AAAA), pin the connection to the resolved address to close the DNS-rebinding gap, set allow_redirects=False (or re-run the check on every hop), and restrict the scheme to http and https explicitly rather than accepting anything urlsplit parses. Where the deployment can, put an egress proxy in front and drop direct outbound from the app container.
findings.verification: Local and authorized only: start your own canary listener on 127.0.0.1:<port>, create a resource pointing at it, request the proxy route, and check whether the canary receives the connection. Any target other than your own canary requires explicit authorization.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the only control on the path is 'has a scheme and a netloc'
triage.FP-08: UNKNOWN for the network layer - a deployment could enforce egress restrictions outside this repository, and no such artifact is present here; per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, not HOLDS, so the network mitigation cannot be credited

findings.open_questions: resourceproxy is not enabled by default; it is enabled on most sites that offer data previews, since ckanext/textview, reclineview and datatablesview all depend on it for cross-domain resources (see ckanext/textview/plugin.py:79, proxy_enabled = p.plugin_loaded('resource_proxy')).

findings.title: The resource proxy reflects the remote server's Content-Type onto the CKAN origin
findings.evidence: response.headers[u'content-type'] = r.headers[u'content-type'] on line 71, where r is the response from the attacker-chosen URL fetched on line 55 or 69. The proxy then streams the remote body into the response (lines 74-76) and returns it from a CKAN route, /dataset/<id>/resource/<resource_id>/proxy. Nothing constrains the type to an inert set, no nosniff header is added, and no Content-Disposition is set. Line 71 also raises KeyError if the remote omits the header, which yields an unhandled 500.
findings.impact: A resource pointing at a server the attacker controls, returning Content-Type: text/html with a script body, renders as a page on the CKAN origin - stored XSS with an attacker-hosted, changeable payload. It is a companion to F6 by a different route: F6 needs the file uploaded, this one needs only a URL.
findings.recommendation: Map the remote type through an allowlist of inert types (text/plain, application/json, text/csv, image/*) and fall back to application/octet-stream; add X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Content-Disposition: attachment on this route; use r.headers.get('content-type', 'application/octet-stream') so a missing header is not a 500.
findings.verification: Local: point a resource at your own local server that returns text/html with an inert marker, request the proxy route and check the response Content-Type and whether the marker executes.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no nosniff, no CSP, no Content-Disposition anywhere in this tree
triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the header comes from a host the resource creator chose

findings.open_questions: Same enablement caveat as F7.

findings.title: No CSRF protection exists; the csrf_input helper is a stub that returns the empty string
findings.impact: Every state-changing route is authorized solely by a credential the browser attaches on its own. The residual risk is governed entirely by one config default, and that is the honest statement of it: who.samesite defaults to 'lax' (ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/auth_tkt.py:99), which in a current browser withholds the auth cookie from a cross-site POST. So on a default install a modern browser blocks the classic attack, and the exposure is (a) any deployment that sets who.samesite=none - a supported, documented option at doc/maintaining/configuration.rst:305-318 - (b) older browsers with no SameSite enforcement, and (c) any same-site subdomain an attacker can reach, which SameSite does not constrain at all. A defence that exists only as a browser default is not the same as one the application enforces, and the stub helper makes the gap invisible to a reviewer who greps for 'csrf' and finds a hit.
findings.recommendation: Either implement the helper for real - generate a per-session token, emit it from csrf_input() into every form macro, and verify it in a before_request that fails closed on unsafe methods - or delete the helper so it stops reading as a control that is present. If the project's position is that SameSite is the defence, say so in the code beside the helper and refuse who.samesite=none the way it already refuses samesite=none without secure (ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/auth_tkt.py:100-103).
findings.verification: Local: from a page on a different origin, submit a form POST to /api/action/package_delete against your instance and observe whether the request is authorized; then repeat with who.samesite=none configured, which is the case that matters.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - SameSite=Lax is a browser behaviour keyed off a config default, not a layer the application enforces and not one that cannot be skipped; FP-01 explicitly excludes a control a caller may forget, and an operator setting who.samesite=none is exactly that
triage.FP-09: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the helper is not something other than it appears; it is named for a control and implements none

findings.open_questions: None. The severity is medium rather than high precisely because of the SameSite default, and that reasoning is stated above rather than hidden in the number.

findings.title: Authentication cookie ships without the Secure attribute and with no absolute expiry by default
findings.evidence: secure = _bool(config.get(u'who.secure', False)) on line 97 - the default is False, and the documentation confirms it is the intended default (doc/maintaining/configuration.rst:292-303, 'Default value: False'). The shipped production template does not set it: grep for who.secure in ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl returns nothing, and the file's only who.* line is a commented-out '# who.timeout = 86400' at line 47. So a default deployment issues the auth_tkt cookie with no Secure attribute and with timeout=None, i.e. no absolute expiry - lines 86-91 only compute a reissue_time when a timeout was configured. Contrast httponly, which defaults to True on line 95, and samesite, which defaults to lax on line 99: the two neighbouring attributes fail safe and this one does not.
findings.impact: Without Secure, the session cookie is attached to any plaintext HTTP request to the same host - a mistyped link, a hard-coded http:// resource URL, an attacker-forced navigation on a shared network - and is captured in transit. Without an absolute timeout, a stolen cookie remains valid indefinitely; there is no server-side expiry to fall back on.
findings.recommendation: Flip the default: make who.secure default to True and require an explicit opt-out for plaintext development, the way samesite=none already requires secure=True at lines 100-103. Set a default who.timeout in ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl rather than shipping it commented out, and add HSTS at the reverse proxy.
findings.verification: Local: log in against an instance using the shipped deployment.ini_tmpl defaults and read the Set-Cookie header for auth_tkt; assert Secure is present in a regression test.

triage.FP-04: DOES_NOT_HOLD - this is the shipped production template, not a development file; I checked ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl specifically for this reason
triage.FP-01: UNKNOWN for HSTS - a reverse proxy could send Strict-Transport-Security and no such artifact exists in this repository; per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, so it cannot be credited as a compensating control

findings.open_questions: None.

findings.title: No rate limiting or account lockout anywhere; login and password reset are unthrottled
findings.evidence: A case-insensitive grep for ratelimit / rate_limit / throttle / lockout across ckan and ckanext, excluding tests, returns nothing: there is no limiter middleware, no per-identity counter and no failed-attempt tracking in the tree. RequestResetView.post is unauthenticated (the login gate at ckan/views/user.py:80-85 exempts request_reset) and sends an email per matching account with no counter - and because the branch at lines 621-635 searches by email and mails *every* account sharing that address, one request can trigger several sends. The login path has no attempt counter either: UsernamePasswordAuthenticator.authenticate (ckan/lib/authenticator.py:17-34) returns None on failure and records nothing. The only anti-automation control in the tree is reCAPTCHA, and it is applied at exactly one call site - ckan/views/user.py:398, user registration - and is inert unless ckan.recaptcha.privatekey is configured, since check_recaptcha returns early when the key is empty (ckan/lib/captcha.py:19-22). The password policy is length >= 8 with no other constraint (ckan/views/user.py:710-724).
findings.impact: Unauthenticated credential stuffing and password brute force against /user/login with no lockout and no delay; unbounded outbound email from /user/reset, which is both a mail-bomb primitive aimed at a chosen victim and a way to burn the deployment's SMTP reputation; and unbounded automated calls to expensive API actions such as package_search. A weak-password policy plus no lockout is a materially different risk from either alone.
findings.recommendation: Add server-side limits keyed on identity as well as IP: a failed-attempt counter with backoff on login bound to the account, a per-address and per-account cap on reset emails, and a general limiter on /api/action with cost proportional to the action. Enforce them in a layer every route passes through rather than per view.
findings.verification: Local: script N failed logins for one account and assert the (N+1)th is refused; script N reset requests for one address and count the messages the mailer produced.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no limiter exists in any layer of this tree
triage.FP-08: UNKNOWN - a WAF or reverse proxy could rate-limit outside this repository and no such artifact is present; per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, not HOLDS

findings.open_questions: None.

findings.title: Password-reset token compared with a non-constant-time equality, and login leaks account existence by timing
findings.evidence: verify_reset_link ends with return key.strip() == user.reset_key on line 219 - a plain Python string comparison, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. The token itself is sound (make_key at line 210-211 is codecs.encode(os.urandom(16), 'hex'), 128 bits from a CSPRNG) and it is rotated after use (ckan/views/user.py:743 calls mailer.create_reset_key again), so the exposure is the comparison, not the token. Note also that the token is stored in the clear in the user row (create_reset_key line 205-207 assigns user.reset_key directly), so a read-only database disclosure yields usable reset tokens. Separately, UsernamePasswordAuthenticator.authenticate (ckan/lib/authenticator.py:20-28) returns as soon as User.by_name(login) is None, without computing a password hash, so a non-existent username is answered measurably faster than an existing one - the pbkdf2_sha512 verification is the dominant cost and it is skipped on that branch.
findings.impact: The timing channel on a 32-hex-character token is not practically exploitable over a network in most deployments, which is why this is low; it is worth fixing because the correct primitive is one line away and the project already uses it elsewhere (passlib.utils.consteq at ckan/model/user.py:130). The login timing difference is a reliable account-existence oracle, which feeds the unthrottled brute force in F11.
findings.recommendation: Use hmac.compare_digest for the reset-token comparison, and store the reset key hashed rather than in the clear. On the login path, compute a dummy password verification when the user is absent so both branches cost the same.
findings.verification: Local: 1000 generated keys checked for uniqueness and entropy against the real code; and a test measuring the authenticate() latency difference between an existing and a non-existing username.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no constant-time wrapper is on this path
triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - key comes from request.params.get('key') at ckan/views/user.py:703
triage.FP-10: HOLDS in part - the timing channel is defence in depth rather than load-bearing given a 128-bit token, which is why the severity is low; the finding is written down rather than dropped, and the login oracle half is not covered by that downgrade

findings.open_questions: I could not measure the timing difference without running the application, so this stays probable rather than confirmed.

findings.title: JSONP wrapping applies to authenticated util endpoints, and the callback is only HTML-escaped
findings.evidence: _finish wraps any 200 GET response in JSONP whenever 'callback' is present in request.args (lines 79-86), escaping the callback with html.escape and setting Content-Type: application/javascript. html.escape neutralises the HTML metacharacters, which is the wrong alphabet for a JavaScript context: a callback of 'x=1;alert' passes through untouched. More importantly, the de-authentication that makes JSONP safe is applied in only one of the two places that reach _finish. action() strips the caller's identity when a callback is present - ckan/views/api.py:270-274 sets g.user, g.userobj and the context user to None - but the util endpoints do not: dataset_autocomplete (line 373), user_autocomplete (line 424), group_autocomplete (line 438) and organization_autocomplete (line 452) all build a context from g.user and then return through _finish_ok, so the JSONP wrapper is applied to a response computed with the caller's session. That asymmetry between two siblings reaching the same sink is the finding.
findings.impact: A third-party page can include <script src="/api/util/user/autocomplete?q=a&callback=steal"> and read the response computed under the victim's session, cross-origin, without CORS. In practice the auth_tkt cookie is not sent on a cross-site subresource load while who.samesite is at its 'lax' default (ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/auth_tkt.py:99), so on a default install this degrades to the anonymous view of those endpoints; it becomes live on any deployment that sets who.samesite=none, and on browsers with no SameSite enforcement.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same de-authentication the action endpoint already performs to every view that can return through _finish, or restrict the JSONP wrapper to side-effect-free anonymous responses. Independently, constrain the callback to ^[A-Za-z_$][A-Za-z0-9_$.]{0,64}$ rather than HTML-escaping it, and keep X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff on these responses.
findings.verification: Local: request /api/util/user/autocomplete?q=a&callback=cb with and without a session cookie and compare the bodies; then repeat as a cross-origin script include from a second local origin.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD as an application control - the de-auth exists at ckan/views/api.py:270 but is not on the util path; SameSite=Lax is a browser default, not a layer the app enforces (same reasoning as F9)
triage.FP-03: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the response is served as application/javascript specifically so it can be executed by an including page
triage.FP-07: UNKNOWN - whether the user list is sensitive depends on the deployment's user_list authorization, which is configurable

findings.open_questions: Whether the anonymous view of user_autocomplete is itself considered sensitive varies by deployment; that is why this is probable and low rather than confirmed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated /_tracking endpoint accepts arbitrary records and crashes on malformed input
findings.evidence: TrackingMiddleware intercepts POST /_tracking before any application routing (lines 68-70) and parses the body by hand: parts = payload.split('&') then, on line 77, k, v = part.split('='). A body part carrying a second '=' raises ValueError ('too many values to unpack'), and a part with none raises the same; neither is caught. Line 82 reads environ['HTTP_USER_AGENT'] by subscript, so a request with no User-Agent header raises KeyError. The identity key is hashlib.md5 over the user agent, remote address and two Accept headers (line 87). The insert on line 93 is correctly parameterised - self.engine.execute(sql, key, data.get('url'), data.get('type')) with %s placeholders - so this is not SQL injection. There is no authentication, no CSRF token and no rate limit on the endpoint.
findings.impact: Three separate small things. An anonymous caller can raise an unhandled exception in middleware with a one-line request, which is a cheap 500 generator and noise in the error channel. An anonymous caller can also write arbitrary url and tracking_type values into tracking_raw at will, inflating or fabricating the view counts that drive the site's popularity ranking (ckan/cli/tracking.py aggregates this table). And MD5 as the anonymisation key is a weak choice for a value derived from low-entropy inputs - the pre-image space of user agent plus IP plus two Accept headers is small enough to enumerate, so the 'anonymised' key does not resist re-identification.
findings.recommendation: Parse with urllib.parse.parse_qs instead of hand-splitting, and use environ.get for every header. Bound the endpoint: a per-key rate limit and a check that the submitted url corresponds to a real object. Replace MD5 with a keyed hash (HMAC-SHA256 with a server secret) if the key is meant to be non-reversible.
findings.verification: Local: POST 'a=b=c' to /_tracking and observe the traceback; POST with no User-Agent header and observe the KeyError; POST an arbitrary url value and read the row it created in tracking_raw.

triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the body and the headers are caller-supplied
triage.FP-07: DOES_NOT_HOLD for the re-identification half - the key is derived from IP and user agent, which PRV-01 would treat as personal
triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - nothing sits in front of this middleware

findings.open_questions: Tracking is off unless ckan.tracking_enabled is set; the middleware is nevertheless installed in the stack in the shipped configuration.

findings.title: markdown_extract sanitises with a hand-rolled regex and marks the result safe, unlike render_markdown
findings.evidence: markdown_extract does plain = RE_MD_HTML_TAGS.sub('', markdown(text)) on line 1437 and then returns literal(plain) on line 1439 (or a truncated literal on 1441-1449). RE_MD_HTML_TAGS is re.compile('<[^><]*>') at line 2323 - a hand-written stripper, not a parser. The asymmetry with its sibling is the finding: render_markdown at line 2367 handles the same class of data and, on the untrusted branch, applies the same regex *and then* bleach_clean with an explicit tag and attribute allowlist (lines 2382-2385). markdown_extract applies the regex and no bleach at all. The inputs are user-controlled - it is called on package.notes, group.description and organization.description from ckan/templates/snippets/package_item.html:19, snippets/group.html:22, snippets/organization.html:44, snippets/organization_item.html:18/20, snippets/group_item.html:19/21, group/snippets/info.html:23 and organization/bulk_process.html:68, i.e. the dataset and group listing pages.
findings.impact: If any input survives the regex as live markup, it becomes stored XSS on the most-visited listing pages in the site. The construct that concerns me is an unterminated tag: '<[^><]*>' requires a closing '>' to match, so a value ending mid-tag is not stripped, and an HTML parser will keep consuming subsequent markup as attributes until it finds a '>' - which reconstructs the element. Whether that reaches the browser depends on whether the Markdown library escapes a stray '<' that starts no well-formed tag, and that is a property of the pinned dependency, not of this tree.
findings.recommendation: Make the two functions use the same sanitiser: run bleach_clean with MARKDOWN_TAGS and MARKDOWN_ATTRIBUTES in markdown_extract too, before the literal(). A regex is not an HTML sanitiser and the codebase already owns the right tool one screen away.
findings.verification: Local: set a group description to '

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no CSP constrains inline execution (F16), and no sanitiser other than the regex is on this path
triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - notes and description are user-supplied
triage.FP-03: UNKNOWN - whether the unterminated-tag input reaches the page as markup depends on the Markdown library's handling of a stray '<', which I could not settle by reading this tree; per the triage invariant this caps the finding at probable

findings.open_questions: Settling FP-03 needs one run of markdown() from the pinned version against the unterminated-tag input. I did not run the application, so I did not settle it, and I am not claiming a bypass I could not construct.

findings.title: No security response headers, and the CORS origin is echoed without Vary alongside public caching
findings.evidence: A grep for Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, nosniff, Referrer-Policy and Strict-Transport-Security across every .py, .ini and .html in ckan and ckanext returns nothing: none of them is ever emitted. The after-request chain at ckan/config/middleware/flask_app.py:407-428 sets only CORS and cache-control. In set_cors_headers_for_response, when the whitelist branch is taken the caller's own Origin is copied into Access-Control-Allow-Origin (lines 82-86) and no Vary: Origin is added - while the very next hook, set_cache_control_headers_for_response (line 98), marks responses public with a max-age drawn from ckan.cache_expires whenever __no_cache__ is absent from the environ.
findings.impact: Three compounding gaps. Without X-Content-Type-Options a browser may sniff an uploaded or proxied response into HTML, which is the sniffing half of F6 and F8. Without a CSP, F5, F6, F8 and F15 all execute unconstrained - a CSP would not close them but would bound them, and its absence is why their severities are not reduced. Without X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors, admin and edit pages are framable for clickjacking. And an echoed Origin with no Vary means a shared cache or CDN can store one origin's Access-Control-Allow-Origin and serve it to another, turning the whitelist into an any-origin policy for cached routes.
findings.recommendation: Add the headers in ckan_after_request: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy unconditionally, frame-ancestors (or X-Frame-Options) on authenticated pages, and a CSP - starting in report-only to find the inline scripts, which F5 shows exist. Add Vary: Origin on every response where the Origin was reflected. Note also that the whitelist branch is only reachable when ckan.cors.origin_allow_all is present-but-false, because the outer gate on line 76 tests the raw config value: a deployment that sets only ckan.cors.origin_whitelist silently emits no CORS headers at all. That fails closed, so it is a correctness bug rather than a vulnerability, but it should be fixed alongside.
findings.verification: Local: curl -sI -H 'Origin: https://example.invalid' against an authenticated route and inspect Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Vary and Cache-Control; assert the header set in a regression test.

triage.FP-08: UNKNOWN for the headers - a reverse proxy could add them outside this repository and no such artifact is present here, so per FP-08 this cannot be credited as HOLDS
triage.FP-10: HOLDS in part - missing headers are defence in depth rather than a vulnerability on their own, which is why this is medium and not high; it stays written down because it is load-bearing for the severity of F5, F6, F8 and F15
triage.FP-07: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the cached responses include authenticated ones

findings.open_questions: None.

findings.title: Unauthenticated snippet route renders test-only templates with caller-supplied variables, gated by an assert
findings.evidence: The route /api/util/snippet/<snippet_path> (registered at ckan/views/api.py:520) prefixes the caller's path with 'ajax_snippets/' and renders it with extra_vars = request.args.to_dict() on line 482 - the entire query string becomes the template context. The path half is bounded (see unaided_pass.dropped: the Flask converter rejects '/' and jinja2's split_template_path rejects '..'), so the reachable set is exactly the three files in ckan/templates/ajax_snippets/. Two of them carry the comment '# Snippet for unit testing ...' - they are test fixtures that ship and are routable in production. The third, follow_button.html, is a single line: {{ h.follow_button(type, id) }}, passing two raw query parameters into the helper. follow_button's only input control is line 1978: assert obj_type in _follow_objects. An assert is not a control - under python -O it is removed entirely, which is WEB-27's named case - and when assertions are on, the AssertionError is unhandled, so a bad type yields a 500 rather than a 400. Omitting the parameters entirely yields a Jinja UndefinedError on the same route.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated 500s on demand, and an input gate that disappears under an interpreter flag. With assertions disabled, obj_type flows unchecked into action = 'am_following_%s' % obj_type and then get_action(action) - a lookup keyed on caller-supplied text against the full action registry. It resolves to a KeyError for anything not named am_following_*, so I can show no reachable action from it, which is why this is low rather than higher; the defect is that the boundary is enforced by a statement the interpreter is allowed to delete. Shipping unit-test fixtures on a public route is unnecessary attack surface in its own right.
findings.recommendation: Replace the assert with an explicit if obj_type not in _follow_objects: raise ValidationError(...). Stop passing request.args wholesale as the template context - accept a declared set of parameters. Move the two unit-test snippets out of the shipped template directory, or gate the route on a testing flag.
findings.verification: Local: GET /api/util/snippet/follow_button.html?type=bogus&id=1 and observe the 500; re-run the same request under python -O and observe that the assert no longer fires.

triage.FP-04: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the route and the fixtures ship; there is no flag gating them
triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - type and id come from request.args
triage.FP-09: DOES_NOT_HOLD - an assert used as a boundary check is exactly WEB-27's named construct
triage.FP-10: HOLDS in part - I could not reach a dangerous action through get_action, so the impact is bounded to the error and the deleted gate; the finding is downgraded, not dropped

findings.open_questions: Whether any third-party extension adds a template under ajax_snippets/ that uses extra_vars less carefully; that is outside this tree.

findings.title: Resource uploads have no content-type check, and the size limit is enforced after the chunk is written
findings.evidence: _copy_file increments current_size once per 1 MB chunk (line 31), writes the chunk (line 37), and only then tests if current_size > max_size (line 39). So the write always precedes the check and the file on disk can exceed the configured maximum by one chunk before the ValidationError aborts. Separately - and this is the larger half - ResourceUpload (ckan/lib/uploader.py:225-300) has no verify_type method and no extension or magic-byte check of any kind; it accepts any content. Its sibling Upload does have one: Upload.verify_type at lines 196-224 reads 2 KB, calls magic.from_buffer and enforces ckan.upload.<object_type>.mimetypes, defaulting to png/gif/jpeg. The gate exists for group and user images and not for resource files - two siblings, one control.
findings.impact: The overrun is minor: bounded at one megabyte per upload and it does not escape the storage directory, since get_directory and get_path (lines 279-296) both realpath-check against the base. The missing type check matters more, because it is the precondition for F6 - an arbitrary body plus an arbitrary declared mimetype is what makes that stored XSS work - and it removes any bound on what the instance stores and later serves.
findings.recommendation: Test the accumulated size before writing the chunk, not after. Give ResourceUpload the same magic-based verification Upload already has, with its own configurable allowlist, so the two upload paths enforce the same class of control.
findings.verification: Local: upload a file just over the configured maximum and measure the bytes written before the abort; upload a file whose magic bytes contradict its declared format and observe that nothing rejects it.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD for the type check - no layer performs it on the resource path; HOLDS for path traversal specifically, since ckan/lib/uploader.py:279-296 canonicalises with realpath before opening, which is why no traversal finding is reported
triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the file content and size are caller-supplied
triage.FP-10: HOLDS for the overrun half - one chunk of slack is defence in depth, not the impact

findings.open_questions: None.

findings.title: Session contents written to the log at debug level
findings.evidence: log.debug(u'Session: %r', session.items()) on line 60, reached from ckan_after_request (ckan/config/middleware/flask_app.py:414) whenever a ckan cookie is present without an authenticated user. The Beaker session dict is dumped whole, including any flash messages queued for the user and whatever an extension has stored in it.
findings.impact: Whatever a plugin puts in the session is copied to the log with no filter. In core the contents are flash messages and session bookkeeping, which is why this is low; the defect is that the statement dumps an open-ended container rather than named fields, so its exposure grows with whatever an extension stores.
findings.recommendation: Log the session id or the key names, not the values.
findings.verification: Local: trigger the branch at DEBUG level with a flash message queued and read the emitted line.

triage.FP-07: UNKNOWN - what the session holds depends on the extensions installed, so I cannot establish that it has no security value; that caps this at probable-to-low rather than dismissing it
triage.FP-04: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the statement ships in the request path

findings.open_questions: None.

findings.title: Datastore error responses return the executed SQL statement and its bound parameters to the caller
findings.evidence: On DBAPIError the handler at lines 1546-1558 returns a ValidationError carrying 'statement': [e.statement], 'params': [e.params] and 'orig': [str(e.orig)] - the server-composed SQL and the bound values, sent back in the API response body. search_sql has the same shape at lines 1620-1628. For datastore_search the statement is composed by CKAN, not by the caller, so what is returned is internal query structure and Postgres error text rather than something the caller already knew.
findings.impact: Reconnaissance: internal column names, the generated query shape and Postgres error detail lower the cost of probing the datastore. For search_sql the caller wrote the SQL, so the disclosure there is close to nil; for datastore_search it is not. Note this is *not* SQL injection - I traced the query construction and the parameterisation holds throughout, including the LIMIT clause interpolation in search_sql, which is bounded by is_single_statement (ckanext/datastore/backend/postgres.py:1970) and the EXPLAIN-based table extraction plus function allowlist at lines 1583-1603.
findings.recommendation: Return a generic message with a correlation id and keep the statement and params in the server log only. Keep the detailed form for search_sql if the project judges it useful there, but not for the structured search path.
findings.verification: Local: call datastore_search with a filter that provokes a database error and read the response body.

triage.FP-05: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the exposure is not bounded or intended for datastore_search
triage.FP-07: DOES_NOT_HOLD - query structure is not public content
triage.FP-10: HOLDS - the impact is reconnaissance rather than a direct compromise, so this is low and informational-leaning; it stays written down

findings.open_questions: One order-of-operations note I could not settle by reading: get_table_and_function_names_from_sql runs EXPLAIN (VERBOSE, FORMAT JSON) on the caller's SQL at ckanext/datastore/helpers.py:102-104, and the function allowlist is only checked afterwards, at ckanext/datastore/backend/postgres.py:1596-1603. Postgres can evaluate immutable functions with constant arguments during planning, so a function could in principle run before it is allowlisted. findings.title: check_recaptcha catches IndexError where the failure raises KeyError
findings.impact: Bounded, and I want to be exact about the direction: a malformed reCAPTCHA response produces an uncaught KeyError, which surfaces as a 500 rather than as a clean CaptchaError. Registration fails either way, so the control fails closed and this is not a bypass. What it costs is a confusing error and a handler that will not do its job the day someone relies on it.
findings.recommendation: Catch KeyError (or use data.get('success')), and keep IndexError only if a list-shaped response is genuinely expected.
findings.verification: Local: point ckan.recaptcha.privatekey at a stub returning JSON with no 'success' key and observe the 500 rather than the CaptchaError.
